headline: A trading account that loses 50% needs a 100% gain just to get back to where it started. A loss and the gain that repairs it are never the same size.

note.line1: A trading account that loses 50% needs a 100% gain just to get back to where it started.
note.line2: A loss and the gain that repairs it are never the same size.
note.caption: After a drawdown, the next gain is earned on a smaller balance. An account that falls from 100 to 50 has to double to return to 100. The gain needed to recover a loss d is d / (1 − d): 11.1% after a 10% loss, 25% after a 20% loss, 100% after a 50% loss. This is why the depth of a drawdown matters more than it first appears.

headline: Is a trading system that wins 90% of its trades always profitable?
topic: trading questions / win rate and expectancy

note.question: Is a trading system that wins 90% of its trades always profitable?
note.caption: No. What a system earns per trade is its expectancy: the win rate times the average win, minus the loss rate times the average loss. A system that wins 90% of the time with an average gain of 1 and an average loss of 10 earns 0.9 × 1 − 0.1 × 10 = −0.1 per trade. Over 100 trades that is 90 wins worth +90 and 10 losses worth −100, a net result of −10. A win rate says how often a system is right, not how much it makes.
note.topic: trading questions / win rate and expectancy

headline: Survivorship bias: The error of judging past market returns only from the funds, stocks or strategies that still exist today, leaving out those that closed or failed. The losers are missing from the data, so the past looks better than it was.

note.text: The error of judging past market returns only from the funds, stocks or strategies that still exist today, leaving out those that closed or failed.
note.line2: The losers are missing from the data, so the past looks better than it was.
note.caption: Funds that perform poorly are more likely to be closed or merged, and companies that fail drop out of an index. A study that keeps only the survivors therefore overstates the average return that was actually available at the time. The same trap appears in trading research when a strategy is tested only on the stocks that make up an index today. A fair test includes everything that existed on each date, including what later disappeared.

headline: Ten losing trades in a row, risking 2% each: −18.3%. Not 20%. Each loss is 2% of a balance that has already shrunk. 0.98 to the power of ten is 0.817.
topic: risk and position sizing / consecutive losses

note.label: Ten losing trades in a row, risking 2% each
note.line1: Not 20%. Each loss is 2% of a balance that has already shrunk.
note.line2: 0.98 to the power of ten is 0.817.
note.caption: When a trader risks a fixed fraction of the current balance, each loss is taken from a smaller amount than the one before. After ten losses of 2% the account keeps 0.98 to the power of ten, about 81.7% of where it started, so the total loss is about 18.3% rather than 20%. Losses expressed as percentages of a changing balance multiply rather than add. The same arithmetic works in the other direction for gains.
note.topic: risk and position sizing / consecutive losses

headline: Myth: After five losing trades in a row, a winning trade is due. Fact: If trades are independent, the chance of a win on the next trade is the same as before the streak.

note.myth: After five losing trades in a row, a winning trade is due.
note.fact: If trades are independent, the chance of a win on the next trade is the same as before the streak.
note.caption: Expecting a reversal after a run of losses is known as the gambler's fallacy. When the outcome of each trade does not depend on the ones before it, a streak carries no information about the next result. A system that wins 40% of its trades still has a 40% chance of winning the sixth trade after five losses. Over many trades the overall ratio moves towards the true win rate because new trades dilute the streak, not because past losses are paid back.

headline: Market order / Limit order. Speed of execution against control of price.
topic: how markets work / market and limit orders

note.line1: Speed of execution against control of price.
note.caption: A market order asks to buy or sell at the best price available when it reaches the market. In a liquid market it is usually filled almost at once, but the final price is not known in advance and can differ from the last quote, especially when prices move fast. A limit order sets the worst price acceptable: a maximum to buy, a minimum to sell. It will never fill at a worse price, but it may fill only in part or not at all if the market does not reach that level.
note.topic: how markets work / market and limit orders

headline: Uncertainty in a measured win rate: SE = √(p(1 − p) / n). 100 trades at a 50% win rate: SE = 5 points. The 95% interval runs from about 40% to 60%.
topic: probability and statistics / standard error of a win rate

note.label: Uncertainty in a measured win rate
note.line1: 100 trades at a 50% win rate: SE = 5 points.
note.line2: The 95% interval runs from about 40% to 60%.
note.caption: A win rate measured over a sample of trades is an estimate, and its standard error is the square root of p(1 − p) / n, where p is the observed win rate and n the number of trades. With 100 trades and a 50% win rate the standard error is 0.05, or 5 percentage points. An approximate 95% interval is the estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors, here about 40% to 60%. Because n sits under a square root, four times as many trades are needed to halve the uncertainty: 400 trades narrow the same interval to about 45% to 55%.
note.topic: probability and statistics / standard error of a win rate

headline: Portfolio Selection, 1952. In 1952 Harry Markowitz published “Portfolio Selection” in the Journal of Finance. It judged a portfolio as a whole, by two numbers: its expected return and the variance of that return.

note.label: Portfolio Selection, 1952
paragraphs: In 1952 Harry Markowitz published “Portfolio Selection” in the Journal of Finance. It judged a portfolio as a whole, by two numbers: its expected return and the variance of that return.
Because assets do not move perfectly together, combining them can lower the risk of the whole without lowering its expected return. Diversification became something that could be measured.
note.caption: Before Markowitz, investment analysis mostly looked at securities one at a time. His 1952 paper in the Journal of Finance proposed choosing a portfolio by the trade-off between expected return and variance, and showed that what matters for risk is how the holdings move together, not only how risky each one is on its own. When returns are less than perfectly correlated, the standard deviation of the combination is lower than the weighted average of the individual standard deviations, while the expected return stays the weighted average. The work became the basis of modern portfolio theory, and Markowitz shared the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1990.

headline: 19 October 1987: −22.6%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 22.6% in one session, its largest one-day percentage decline. Black Monday. 508 points in one day.

note.text: The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 22.6% in one session, its largest one-day percentage decline.
note.line2: Black Monday. 508 points in one day.
note.caption: On Monday 19 October 1987 the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 508 points, from 2,246.74 to 1,738.74, a decline of 22.6% in one session. It remains the largest one-day percentage fall in the history of the index. Stock markets around the world fell sharply in the same days. A single session erased more than a fifth of the index value, far outside the range of ordinary daily moves. Source: Federal Reserve History; Dow Jones Industrial Average closing values, 1987.

headline: An average return of 0% still lost a quarter of capital. Compound rate: −13.4% a year.

note.line1: An average return of 0% still lost a quarter of capital.
note.caption: A portfolio that gains 50% and then loses 50% has an arithmetic average return of 0%, yet it ends at 75 for every 100 it started with. The loss is taken on a larger base than the gain, so swings cost money even when they cancel on paper. The rate that actually describes the path is the geometric mean: the square root of 0.75, minus one, or about −13.4% a year. This gap between the two averages is called volatility drag, and it grows with the size of the swings.

headline: Win rate / Losing run of 5+. Chance of at least five losses in a row over 100 independent trades.

head: Win rate
Losing run of 5+
note.line1: Chance of at least five losses in a row over 100 independent trades.
note.caption: A losing streak is not by itself evidence that a system has stopped working. If each trade is independent and wins with a fixed probability, the chance of at least one run of five or more consecutive losses somewhere in 100 trades is about 98% at a 40% win rate, 81% at 50%, 46% at 60% and 15% at 70%. The figures are exact results of the standard recursion for runs in independent trials, the same mathematics as the longest run of heads in repeated coin tosses. The longest run of losses grows roughly with the logarithm of the number of trades, so longer samples contain longer streaks.

headline: One trade shows the outcome, not the quality of the decision. A process can only be judged over many trades.
topic: systematic trading philosophy / process over outcome

note.line1: One trade shows the outcome, not the quality of the decision.
note.line2: A process can only be judged over many trades.
note.caption: Every trade has two separate qualities: whether the rules were followed, and whether it made money. A trade taken by the rules can lose, because no sound system wins every time, and a trade that breaks the rules can still win by chance. Judging a decision by its result alone is known as outcome bias, and its most costly case is the lucky win, which rewards a mistake and makes it more likely to be repeated. Over a large number of trades, results reflect the process; over a single trade, they mostly reflect chance.
note.topic: systematic trading philosophy / process over outcome

headline: Past the optimum, more risk per trade means slower growth. Growth peaks at 25% risked and is zero at 50%.
topic: risk and position sizing / growth rate against position size

note.label: Long-run growth against risk per trade
note.line1: Past the optimum, more risk per trade means slower growth.
note.line2: Growth peaks at 25% risked and is zero at 50%.
note.caption: Consider a system that wins half its trades, with each win twice the size of each loss, and a fixed fraction of capital risked on every trade. The long-run compound growth rate is 0.5 × ln(1 + 2f) + 0.5 × ln(1 − f), where f is the fraction risked. It peaks at 25%, the Kelly fraction for this edge, falls back to zero at 50%, and is negative beyond that, so capital shrinks over time despite the positive expectancy. Risking 12.5% or 37.5% gives exactly the same growth rate, but the larger size carries far deeper drawdowns.
note.topic: risk and position sizing / growth rate against position size

headline: Four ways a backtest can mislead: Survivorship: testing only on assets that still exist today Look-ahead: using data that was not yet known at the time Data snooping: trying many rules and keeping the best one Costs: leaving out spreads, commissions and slippage

note.label: Four ways a backtest can mislead
items: Survivorship: testing only on assets that still exist today
Look-ahead: using data that was not yet known at the time
Data snooping: trying many rules and keeping the best one
Costs: leaving out spreads, commissions and slippage
note.caption: A backtest replays rules on past prices, and small errors in how it is built can make a weak system look strong. Survivorship bias comes from testing only on assets that survived, leaving out those that were delisted or failed. Look-ahead bias appears when a rule uses information that was only available later, such as revised data or the closing price of the same bar. Data snooping is the result of testing many variations and reporting only the best, which tends to fit noise. Ignoring trading costs inflates every result, most of all for systems that trade often.
